title: Halogens (Group 7)
keyIdea: The halogens are fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine. They exist as pairs of atoms (Cl₂, Br₂). Going down the group, melting and boiling points rise and colours darken: two gases, then a liquid, then a solid. Each atom has 7 outer electrons and reacts by gaining one. Reactivity falls down the group because the outer shell is further from the nucleus. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.

kid: Group 7 is a family of elements called the halogens. Fluorine and chlorine are gases. Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Iodine is a grey-black solid.
Each halogen atom has 7 electrons in its outer shell. It needs just one more to fill it. So halogens grab an electron from other atoms.
Fluorine grabs hardest. Its outer shell sits close to the middle of the atom, so the pull is strong. Further down, the shell is further out and the pull is weaker.
A strong grabber can steal from a weak one. Put chlorine in a salt that has bromine in it. The chlorine takes the electron, and orange bromine appears.
adult: The halogens are diatomic: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂. Down the group the molecules get larger, so the forces between molecules get stronger and melting and boiling points rise. Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine a yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid with a purple vapour.

Every halogen atom has 7 outer electrons and reacts by gaining one to form a −1 ion: chlorine becomes chloride, Cl⁻. Down the group each atom has an extra shell. The outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so an incoming electron is attracted less strongly. Reactivity therefore falls from fluorine to iodine.

In a displacement reaction a more reactive halogen takes electrons from the ions of a less reactive one: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Chlorine displaces bromine and iodine, bromine displaces iodine, and iodine displaces neither. The colour shows the product: bromine in water is orange and iodine is brown.

Watch for common mistakes. Group 7 reactivity falls down the group, the opposite of Group 1, because halogens gain electrons while alkali metals lose them. Chloride is not chlorine. Bromine water added to potassium chloride stays orange, but nothing has reacted. Fluorine is the most reactive even though measured electron affinity is slightly higher for chlorine; its weak F–F bond and strong bonds to other atoms explain this.

familyTip: Play 'steal the sock'. A strong player can take a sock from a weaker one, but not the other way round. Rank three players. Who can steal from whom? Halogens work the same way with electrons.

worked.title: Predict what happens when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution, and write the ionic equation.
steps: Find both halogens in Group 7: bromine is above iodine, so bromine is more reactive.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt, so a reaction happens.
Each Br₂ takes two electrons, one from each of two I⁻ ions: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.
The solution turns brown as iodine forms. Potassium ions are spectators and do not appear in the ionic equation.

practice.prompt: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution. What happens?
choices: Iodine is made and the solution turns brown
Chlorine is made and the solution turns green
practice.hint: Which is higher in Group 7, chlorine or iodine?
practice.explain: Chlorine is more reactive, so it takes electrons from I⁻: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. Iodine in solution is brown.

practice.hint: Chlorine above it is a gas and iodine below it is a solid.
practice.explain: Bromine melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C, so it is a red-brown liquid at about 20 °C.

practice.prompt: In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, how many Br⁻ ions lose an electron when {n} chlorine molecules react?
practice.hint: Each Cl₂ molecule gains two electrons, one from each of two Br⁻ ions.
practice.explain: Each Cl₂ needs 2 electrons, so {n} molecules take electrons from 2 × {n} = {=2*n} Br⁻ ions.

practice.prompt: Why does reactivity decrease down Group 7?
choices: The atoms have more protons, which repel electrons
The outer shell is further from the nucleus, so a new electron is attracted less strongly
The atoms lose electrons less easily
practice.hint: Halogens react by gaining an electron. What makes that harder lower down?
practice.explain: Each element down the group has an extra shell. The outer shell is further out and more shielded, so the pull on an incoming electron is weaker.

practice.prompt: {n} bromine molecules react completely with iodide ions. How many iodine molecules form?
practice.hint: Use Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂ and compare the numbers in front of Br₂ and I₂.
practice.explain: One Br₂ makes one I₂, so {n} Br₂ molecules make {n} I₂ molecules.

pool.prompt: Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution. It stays orange. Why?
choices: There is no reaction: the orange is the bromine that was added
Potassium chloride turns orange when mixed with water
pool.hint: Is bromine more or less reactive than chlorine?
pool.explain: Bromine is below chlorine, so it cannot displace it. The orange colour is just the bromine water.

pool.prompt: Which halogen is the most reactive?
pool.hint: Reactivity falls going down the group.
pool.explain: Fluorine is at the top. Its outer shell is closest to the nucleus, so it gains an electron most readily.

pool.prompt: Astatine is below iodine. What does the trend predict about it?
choices: A pale gas that is more reactive than iodine
A dark solid that is less reactive than iodine
pool.hint: Follow two trends: state and colour, and reactivity.
pool.explain: Colours darken and melting points rise down the group, and reactivity falls, so astatine should be a dark solid less reactive than iodine.

pool.prompt: {n} chlorine molecules displace bromine from potassium bromide. How many chloride ions form?
pool.hint: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Each Cl₂ gives two Cl⁻.
pool.explain: Each Cl₂ molecule becomes two Cl⁻ ions, so {n} molecules give {=2*n} chloride ions.

pool.prompt: Which is the correct ionic equation for chlorine reacting with iodide ions?
pool.hint: Halogens are diatomic, and the more reactive halogen ends up as the ion.
pool.explain: Chlorine is more reactive, so it becomes chloride ions and iodine is released as I₂. The third equation runs the wrong way.

pool.prompt: Down Group 1 reactivity increases, but down Group 7 it decreases. Why the difference?
choices: Alkali metals react by losing an electron; halogens react by gaining one
pool.hint: A distant outer electron is easy to lose but hard to attract.
pool.explain: A further-out outer shell makes losing an electron easier (Group 1) but gaining one harder (Group 7).

pool.prompt: What is the difference between chlorine and chloride?
choices: They are two names for the same thing
Chlorine is the element, Cl₂; chloride is the ion, Cl⁻, found in salts
Chloride is chlorine gas dissolved in water
pool.hint: Look at the charge. Which one has gained an electron?
pool.explain: Chlorine is a toxic gas made of Cl₂ molecules. Chloride ions in table salt have each gained an electron and are harmless.

pool.prompt: How do halogen atoms usually exist as elements?
choices: As single atoms, like noble gases
As molecules of two atoms, such as Br₂
pool.hint: Two halogen atoms can share electrons to each get 8.
pool.explain: Two atoms share a pair of electrons in a covalent bond, so the elements are F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.

pool.prompt: Iodine solution is added to potassium bromide solution. What do you see?
choices: It turns orange as bromine forms
pool.hint: Can a less reactive halogen displace a more reactive one?
pool.explain: Iodine is below bromine, so it cannot take electrons from Br⁻. The brown colour is the iodine solution added.

pool.prompt: Chlorine water is added to excess potassium iodide. If {n} chlorine molecules react, how many iodine molecules form?
pool.hint: Write Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ and compare Cl₂ with I₂.
pool.explain: One Cl₂ releases one I₂, so {n} chlorine molecules release {n} iodine molecules, turning the solution brown.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: slide down Group 7, drop an electron into chlorine, and pour halogens into salt solutions to find which reactions happen.
